query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the element X controls whether a stable oxide scale forms at temperatures above 900 °C by governing the kinetics and chemistry of oxide layer development; specifically, when X is Al or Si rather than Mn, the slower diffusion and stronger affinity for oxygen promotes the formation of a coherent, adherent alumina or silica-based oxide that limits internal oxidation and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys processed to obtain a single-phase or well‐distributed multiphase metallic solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Alter the alloying element X by preparing otherwise identical CrFeCoNiX compositions with X = Al, Si, or Mn.
generation.conditions: Exposing the alloys in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 950–1000 °C) for an extended period.
generation.structural_mediator: The diffusional behavior of the X element and its resulting oxide (e.g., dense Al2O3 or SiO2) formation at the alloy surface, which influences the oxide layer microstructure and its adhesion to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: For alloys with Al or Si, these elements diffuse to the surface at high temperature and form stable, low-growth-rate oxides that develop into coherent protective layers. In contrast, when Mn is the dominant reactive element, faster diffusion and formation of less stable, more voluminous oxides lead to stress build-up, cracking, and spallation of the protective film.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will develop thinner, more uniform, and adherent protective oxide films, while alloys with X = Mn will exhibit thicker, irregular, and cracked/spalled oxide layers.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNiMn alloy (with X = Mn), which is expected to produce less protective, unstable oxide scales due to the nature of manganese oxides.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid solution state exposed to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive environments; deviations in microstructure, non-equilibrium processing routes, or different temperature regimes could alter oxide behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in oxide layer thickness and adhesion may depend on processing parameters, minor element segregation, and exact alloy compositions; further detailed studies are needed to establish threshold levels of Al or Si necessary for optimal oxide stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X systematically varied among Al, Si, and Mn while keeping processing and microstructure constant. Expose samples in a controlled oxidative atmosphere at 950 °C for 24 hours. Conduct cross-sectional analysis of the oxide layers using SEM, EDS, and XRD, and perform adhesion/spallation testing.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via SEM cross-sections)
Phase identification and composition of the oxides (using XRD and EDS)
Adhesion strength of the oxide film (via standardized pull-off or scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-containing alloy forms an oxide scale with comparable coherence, composition, and adhesion as observed in the Al- or Si-containing alloys, then the hypothesis that the nature of X governs protective oxide formation through diffusion kinetics and oxide stability is falsified.

Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Microstructure Evolution of FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 High Entropy Alloy during Powder Preparation, Laser Powder Bed Fusion, and Microplasma Spraying

Abstract: AbstractIn the present study, powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was manufactured by gas atomization process, and then used for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and microplasma spraying (MPS) technologies. The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata

Abstract: AbstractTogether with the thermodynamics and kinetics, the complex microstructure of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exerts a significant influence on the associated oxidation mechanisms in these concentrated solid solutions. To describe the surface oxidation in AlCoCrFeNi HEA, we employed a stochastic cellular automata model that replicates the mesoscale structures that form. The model benefits from diffusion coefficients of the principal elements through the native oxides predicted by using molecular simulations. Through our examination of the oxidation behavior as a function of the alloy composition, we corroborated that the oxide scale growth is a function of the complex chemistry and resultant microstructures. The effect of heat treatment on these alloys is also simulated by using reconstructed experimental micrographs. When they are in a single-crystal structure, no segregation is noted for α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, which are the primary scale-forming oxides.
